newsitem.title: VIETNAM: US, Vietnam agree on debt deal but differ on future.
newsitem.headline: US, Vietnam agree on debt deal but differ on future.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin hailed the signing on Monday of a pact to reschedule Vietnam's debt as a significant step, but said it would take time for the war-time foes to forge closer economic ties.

Rubin, the highest ranking U.S. economic official to visit here since the war ended in 1975, urged Hanoi to press ahead with its market reforms, saying that was the way for it to win trade concessions and financing from Washington.
"There is a lot Vietnam can do -- and do quickly," he told the U.S.-Vietnam Trade Council.
However Rubin's message did not seem to go down well with Vietnamese policymakers.

In his speech to the Council, Vietnamese Deputy Foreign Minister Nguyen Dinh Bin said there was a limit to what Hanoi could do on its own and made clear he felt the United States bore the main responsibility for forging closer ties.
"It would be unfair to set forth requirements beyond Vietnam's real ability and higher than those for other countries," Bin said.
"We ... hope that the United States will take more positive measures to speed up this (economic normalisation) process," he added.

The two countries cleared a hurdle to broaden economic ties with their signing on Monday of an agreement to reschedule $145 million in debts that Hanoi inherited from the U.S.-backed Saigon government after the Vietnam War.
Under the pact, Hanoi was given until 2019 to repay the four development loans and two food credits incurred by its former enemy in the south.
"This agreement removes an important obstacle to closer ties between the United States and Vietnam," Rubin said. "This is a significant step."

The Treasury chief, who held separate meetings with Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet and Finance Minister Nguyen Sinh Hung, said his visit signified a shift in the relationship from conflict to cooperation.

The next step is a trade agreement between the two countries. But for that to come about, Vietnam must make substantial commitments to open up its markets and treat foreign companies the same as Vietnamese ones, he said.

A trade deal is one condition needed for communist Vietnam to earn Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status from the United States. MFN, which guarantees non-discriminatory tariffs on exports, would give Vietnam access to the world's largest consumer market.

Rubin told reporters he had discussed MFN in meetings with Kiet and Hung, but had not focused on the question of when it would be granted. The two sides are scheduled to resume negotiations next week.
"These things by their nature take time," he said. "They are complicated."
He said Vietnam, which began experimenting with economic reforms more than a decade ago, had made great strides but added that further progress on opening its market would inevitably be slow.
"I was impressed with the commitments the finance minister expressed this morning, and that the prime minister has expressed to move into a market economy," he said.
Rubin's visit is part of the sometimes painstaking process of mending relations. The United States normalised diplomatic relations only in May 1995.
